opts: Correct. Lymphoma staging is based on the Lugano classification, a modified version of the older Ann Arbor system, which stages by the involved node regions and organs relative to the diaphragm.
The Rai classification stages chronic lymphocytic leukemia from the exam and labs. Tell: Rai is for the leukemia; Lugano is for lymphoma.
The Revised International Staging System stages multiple myeloma with beta-2 microglobulin, albumin, chromosomes and lactate dehydrogenase. Tell: that is myeloma staging.

set1.q: What produces the starry sky appearance of Burkitt lymphoma?
opts: Correct. The starry sky appearance is sheets of lymphoma cells with benign macrophages that are clearing out the dying lymphoma cells. The pale macrophages are the stars against the dark sheet of tumor.
Binucleated neoplastic B cells (Reed-Sternberg cells) among many immune cells define Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: few large binucleated cells mean Hodgkin; macrophages in sheets mean Burkitt.
Clusters of packed follicles are the microscopy of follicular lymphoma. Tell: follicles mean follicular; starry sky means Burkitt.
Plasma cells, terminally differentiated B cells, give rise to the plasma cell disorders such as multiple myeloma. Tell: plasma cells mean myeloma.

Referral to and management by a hematologist/oncologist is required, even for a patient who is only being observed. Tell: watch and wait is still specialist-led.
Radiation is a treatment for a single-node, non-aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma, not the core of this leukemia's care. Tell: the referral is to hematology/oncology.

opts: Myeloma is considered incurable, and each line of therapy gives shorter remissions. Tell: the aim is long remission, not cure.
Myeloma is by definition symptomatic; it is smoldering myeloma, a more indolent process, that is often monitored. Tell: active myeloma is treated.
Eradication is not the stated aim; the disease remains incurable and relapsing. Tell: prolong remission, protect quality of life.
Long remissions and quality of life
Correct. Because myeloma is by definition symptomatic and considered incurable, the goal of treatment is maintaining prolonged remissions to improve survival while maintaining quality of life.

One course of therapy cures it

set1.q: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma is associated with which infection?
opts: Correct. Splenic marginal zone lymphoma is associated with hepatitis C. Marginal zone lymphomas make up 5-17% of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, are more common in older adults, and the gastric extranodal form is tied to H. pylori.
Helicobacter pylori is linked to gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma, the extranodal subtype. Tell: H. pylori is the stomach; hepatitis C is the spleen.
Human immunodeficiency virus is tied to immunodeficiency-associated Burkitt lymphoma and is a general lymphoma risk. Tell: the splenic marginal zone association is hepatitis C.

opts: The Caribbean, Central America and South America are where adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, linked to human T-lymphotropic virus 1, is more common. Tell: Caribbean origin points to that T-cell lymphoma, not to chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

African Americans carry a higher risk of multiple myeloma than other races. The group named for chronic lymphocytic leukemia is Eastern European and Jewish descent. Tell: African American race is a stated risk for multiple myeloma.
Sub-Saharan Africa and New Guinea are where endemic Burkitt lymphoma, strongly tied to Epstein-Barr virus, is seen. Tell: sub-Saharan Africa means endemic Burkitt, not chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

set1.q: Which chromosomal translocation causes follicular lymphoma?
opts: Correct. Follicular lymphoma arises from the t(14;18) translocation, which places the B-cell lymphoma 2 gene on chromosome 14 and prevents cell death. Microscopy often shows clusters of packed follicles.
The t(11;14) translocation is not the one that places the B-cell lymphoma 2 gene on chromosome 14 to prevent cell death. Tell: 14;18 is follicular.

Four times understates the sibling risk, which is 10 times. Tell: the same-sex sibling figure is ten.

set1.q: Outside of lymphoma, in which setting can tumor lysis syndrome also be seen?
opts: Monoclonal B lymphocytosis is an elevated lymphocyte count below 5,000 with no lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, cytopenias or symptoms. Tell: tumor lysis needs rapid tumor breakdown.

Correct. Tumor lysis syndrome can be seen outside lymphomas, in acute lymphocytic leukemia and acute myelogenous leukemia with marked leukocytosis. Within lymphoma it can occur spontaneously in highly aggressive types such as Burkitt.

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance is an asymptomatic plasma cell condition with a low risk of progression, not a rapidly breaking-down tumor. Tell: tumor lysis needs rapid tumor breakdown.

Follicular lymphoma is indolent and frequently needs no treatment (watch and wait), so there is no rapid tumor breakdown. Tell: tumor lysis follows rapid breakdown, as in aggressive lymphomas or leukemia with a high count.

opts: The disease involves the blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen. Tell: the favorable outlook comes from elderly onset and novel agents, not from sparing the marrow.

Correct. Ongoing development of novel therapies (such as cellular and bispecific antibody therapies) and the elderly age at onset, median 70 years, mean many patients will die with chronic lymphocytic leukemia rather than from it.
Spontaneous regression is not described; asymptomatic disease is watched until rapid progression or symptoms. Tell: the reasons are age at onset and novel therapies.

set1.q: Under the R-ISS (Revised International Staging System), a myeloma patient who meets neither stage I nor stage III criteria is which stage?
opts: Stage I requires every favorable criterion: beta-2 microglobulin under 3.5 mg/L, albumin at least 3.5 g/dL, standard-risk chromosomes and normal lactate dehydrogenase. Tell: missing stage I makes it II or III.

Correct. In the R-ISS (Revised International Staging System), stage II is defined as not stage I or III. Stage I needs low beta-2 microglobulin, normal albumin, standard-risk chromosomes and normal lactate dehydrogenase; stage III needs high beta-2 microglobulin with high-risk chromosomes and high lactate dehydrogenase.
Stage III requires beta-2 microglobulin of 5.5 mg/L or more with high-risk chromosomes and high lactate dehydrogenase. Tell: not meeting stage III leaves stage II.

T-cell lymphomas respond less well than B-cell lymphomas, so a B-cell type is not the adverse factor. Tell: T-cell is worse.

opts: A marrow biopsy is not needed for Rai staging and is usually not needed for diagnosis either. Tell: the stage comes from the exam and the blood counts.
Cytogenetics inform prognosis and some treatment choices but are not part of the Rai stage. Tell: Rai uses nodes, organs, hemoglobin and platelets, not chromosomes.

opts: Only 5-10% of patients develop B symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fevers), so they are not the usual route to diagnosis. Tell: most patients have no symptoms at all when the count is found.
Thrombocytopenia can cause easy bruising and bleeding, but most patients are asymptomatic when diagnosed. Tell: bleeding is a cytopenia symptom, not the common first clue.

A very rapidly growing swelling, with changes visible during the course of one day, describes Burkitt lymphoma, a very aggressive lymphoma. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia nodes are painless, firm and mobile, and the disease is often silent. Tell: rapid growth means Burkitt.

opts: A bone marrow biopsy is usually not required to diagnose chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: the blood itself is examined by flow cytometry to show the clone.

Excisional lymph node biopsy is how a lymphoma is diagnosed, because the node architecture must be seen. This leukemia is confirmed from the blood. Tell: node biopsy is for lymphoma; flow cytometry is for this leukemia.

Serum protein electrophoresis shows the monoclonal protein of multiple myeloma and the other plasma cell disorders. Tell: a monoclonal protein means a plasma cell disorder; a clonal B-cell population on flow means chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

Correct. With early identification and multi-agent chemotherapy, long-term prognosis is excellent: above 90% in children and 50-90% in adults. Prompt treatment with emergent hematology referral is the key.

Observation (watch and wait) suits asymptomatic follicular lymphoma, not relapsed Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: relapse after first-line therapy escalates to transplant.

Autologous transplant followed by maintenance therapy is the step shown to improve overall survival in transplant-eligible multiple myeloma; for Hodgkin lymphoma that relapses after first-line treatment, the transplant named is allogeneic. set1.q: In tumor lysis syndrome, which released product carries the largest risk of death?
opts: Uric acid precipitates in the renal tubules and causes acute renal failure, which allopurinol helps prevent. Tell: uric acid harms the kidney; potassium causes the fatal arrhythmia.
Calcium phosphate crystals form in the tubules, but calcium itself is not the released product named as the largest risk. Tell: hyperkalemia drives the arrhythmia.

Correct. Tumor lysis syndrome releases potassium, phosphorus and uric acid; the largest risk is hyperkalemia, which leads to arrhythmia and potential death. It is a medical emergency needing aggressive intravenous fluids.

opts: A lymphocyte count below 5,000 with no nodes, organomegaly or cytopenias is monoclonal B lymphocytosis. Tell: that is a lymphocyte clone, not a plasma cell clone.
M-protein under 3 g/dL, plasma cells under 10%

Correct. MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance) is by definition asymptomatic: M-protein below 3 g/dL, clonal bone marrow plasma cells below 10% and no myeloma-defining characteristics. It progresses to myeloma at about 1% per year.

An M-protein above 3 g/dL with 10-60% marrow plasma cells and no myeloma-defining events is smoldering myeloma. Tell: higher numbers without CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) features mean smoldering.
Plasma cells 10% or more with bone lesions

set1.q: What causes the renal dysfunction of multiple myeloma?
opts: Osteoclast activation releases calcium into the bloodstream; the kidney injury itself is named as light chain and calcium phosphate deposition. Tell: osteoclasts raise calcium; the main kidney injury named is light chain deposition.
Correct. Renal dysfunction in myeloma often comes from light chain and calcium phosphate deposition. Anemia is multifactorial, from renal dysfunction and bone marrow involvement.
Uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals in the tubules cause the renal failure of tumor lysis syndrome. Tell: uric acid is tumor lysis; light chains are myeloma.
Hyperviscosity is not the named cause of myeloma kidney injury, which is light chain and calcium phosphate deposition. Tell: myeloma kidneys clog with light chains.

opts: Hodgkin lymphoma spreads contiguously in an orderly fashion, not by skipping. Tell: orderly is the key word.
Skin lesions that resemble fungal infections are the presentation of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Tell: Hodgkin spreads node to adjacent node.
Osteolytic, punched-out bone lesions are a feature of multiple myeloma. Tell: Hodgkin spreads through contiguous nodes.

set1.q: Why is fine needle aspiration avoided when lymphoma is suspected?
opts: Seeding is not the reason given; aspiration is avoided because it cannot show the node's architecture and may miss the diagnosis. Tell: the problem is too little tissue.
Tumor lysis syndrome comes from rapid tumor breakdown, which can occur spontaneously in highly aggressive lymphomas, not from a needle. Tell: the concern is a missed diagnosis.
The reason given is diagnostic, not procedural: the needle sample loses the node architecture. Tell: architecture decides the method.

Correct. Fine needle aspiration is avoided because an excisional biopsy is required to observe the lymph node architecture, and aspiration may miss the diagnosis. Biopsy is reserved for significant (2 cm), persistent and progressively enlarging nodes.

opts: Correct. Monoclonal B lymphocytosis, a count below 5,000 with no nodes, organomegaly, cytopenias or symptoms, progresses to chronic lymphocytic leukemia at a rate of 1-2% per year.
About 10% per year is the progression rate of smoldering myeloma to multiple myeloma. Tell: 10% belongs to smoldering myeloma; 1-2% to monoclonal B lymphocytosis.
A quarter per year overstates the risk; monoclonal B lymphocytosis progresses at only 1-2% per year. Tell: it is a low-risk precursor.

set1.q: How is tumor lysis syndrome prevented before treating an aggressive lymphoma?
opts: Tumor lysis releases potassium, and hyperkalemia is its greatest danger, so extra potassium is the opposite of prevention. Tell: the goal is clearing products, not adding potassium.
Aggressive lymphomas, especially Burkitt, need prompt treatment; prevention means preparing with fluids and allopurinol, not waiting. Tell: anticipate and protect, then treat.
Tumor lysis syndrome requires aggressive intravenous fluid hydration; restricting fluids would worsen crystal precipitation. Tell: give fluids, never restrict them.

The t(4;14) translocation is a high-risk abnormality in the myeloma staging table. Tell: it marks high-risk myeloma, not a lymphoma.

opts: Forty is far too young for the median; chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a disease of older adults with a median age of 70 years. Tell: think of an older adult found on routine blood work, not a young adult.
Fifty-five falls well short of the median age of 70 years for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: the median sits a decade above 60, not below it.

Correct. The median age at diagnosis, and at onset, of chronic lymphocytic leukemia is 70 years, so it is a disease of older adults. That elderly onset is one reason many patients are expected to die with the disease rather than from it.
Eighty-five overshoots; the median age at diagnosis is 70 years. Tell: the median is 70, so half of patients are diagnosed younger than that.

set2.q: Which regimen is an example of multi-drug therapy for aggressive B-cell lymphoma?
opts: Venetoclax plus obinutuzumab for a fixed duration

Venetoclax, a B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitor, combined with a monoclonal antibody such as obinutuzumab for a fixed duration is a chronic lymphocytic leukemia targeted therapy. Tell: that is a leukemia combination; aggressive lymphoma gets rituximab with CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone).
Rituximab plus CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone)

Correct. Aggressive B-cell lymphomas are often treated with multi-drug chemotherapy such as R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, prednisone). Rituximab is the anti-cluster of differentiation 20 monoclonal antibody.
ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) without rituximab

ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) was historically the short course of chemotherapy for early-stage Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: that regimen is Hodgkin; rituximab with CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) is aggressive B-cell.
CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) without rituximab

CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) without rituximab is the similar regimen used for T-cell lymphomas, because T cells have no cluster of differentiation 20; it leaves out the rituximab of the B-cell example. Tell: a B-cell lymphoma keeps the rituximab.

set2.q: Burkitt lymphoma is associated with upregulation of which gene?
opts: Correct. Burkitt lymphoma is associated with MYC (myelocytomatosis oncogene) upregulation, which stimulates cell growth and division. That explains a swelling that can visibly enlarge over one day.
BCL-2 (B-cell lymphoma 2) is moved to chromosome 14 by t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma, preventing cell death. Tell: the cell-death gene is follicular; Burkitt is the growth gene.
Cyclin D1 translocation t(11;14) identifies mantle cell lymphoma. Tell: cyclin D1 is mantle cell.
MYD88 (myeloid differentiation primary response 88) mutation is found in about 90% of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Tell: that marks Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, not Burkitt.

set2.q: What causes the hypercalcemia of multiple myeloma?
opts: Tumor lysis releases potassium, phosphorus and uric acid, not calcium from bone. Tell: myeloma calcium comes from bone resorption.
Renal dysfunction in myeloma comes from light chain and calcium phosphate deposition; the calcium itself comes from bone. Tell: osteoclasts are the source.

Correct. Myeloma activates osteoclasts, resulting in calcium release into the bloodstream. Hypercalcemia causes constipation, increased thirst, urinary frequency and nausea, and osteolytic, punched-out lesions are the bone finding.
Light chain and calcium phosphate deposition cause the renal dysfunction of myeloma, not the hypercalcemia. Tell: light chains hit the kidney; osteoclasts release the calcium.

set2.q: How is a single-node, non-aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma treated?
opts: Allopurinol and fluids prevent tumor lysis syndrome before aggressive lymphoma treatment; they do not treat the lymphoma. Tell: prevention, not therapy.

Correct. Management depends heavily on subtype and presentation; a single-node, non-aggressive lymphoma is treated with radiation. Aggressive B-cell lymphomas instead get multi-drug chemotherapy with rituximab.
Multi-drug chemotherapy is the approach to aggressive B-cell lymphomas. Tell: one node and non-aggressive means radiation.
Autologous transplant improves survival in transplant-eligible multiple myeloma. Tell: transplant belongs to myeloma; a single indolent node gets radiation.

set2.q: When used as monotherapy, how long is a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor usually given?
opts: No count-based stopping point is given; the drug is usually continuous as monotherapy. Tell: monotherapy is open-ended.
Kinase inhibitor monotherapy is not stopped when symptoms improve; it is usually continuous. Tell: continuous, not symptom-guided.
Correct. Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib) are usually continuous when used as monotherapy. Time-limited courses belong to the combination regimens.
A fixed duration describes venetoclax combined with monoclonal antibodies. Tell: kinase inhibitor monotherapy keeps going.

set2.q: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma cells express which pair of cluster of differentiation markers?
opts: Cluster of differentiation 19 belongs to the chronic lymphocytic leukemia pair (with 5). Tell: Hodgkin pairs 30 with 15.

Correct. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma expresses cluster of differentiation 15 and cluster of differentiation 30. The diagnosis itself is made by excisional lymph node biopsy, avoiding fine needle aspiration.
Coexpression of cluster of differentiation 19 and 5 identifies chronic lymphocytic leukemia on flow cytometry. Tell: 19 and 5 are the leukemia; 15 and 30 are Hodgkin.
Cluster of differentiation 20 is the rituximab target on B cells and 5 is part of the chronic lymphocytic leukemia pair. Tell: classical Hodgkin is 15 and 30.

set2.q: Which statement belongs in education for a patient newly diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: Admission is needed to start therapy
Hospital admission is described for aggressive lymphomas with electrolyte abnormalities, not for this leukemia. Tell: chronic lymphocytic leukemia care is outpatient pills or infusions.
No follow-up is needed once stable
Patients will require follow-ups for lab monitoring and treatment. Tell: monitoring continues even when the outlook is good.
The long-term prognosis is likely very good, with 5-year relative survival about 88%. Tell: poor outcomes belong to Richter transformation, not to the usual course.

Correct. Patients are unlikely to require hospitalization, and treatment is likely based on patient preferences and mutations. They will need follow-up for lab monitoring and treatment, but the long-term prognosis is likely very good.

set2.q: What is Bence Jones protein?
opts: A monoclonal protein on serum protein electrophoresis is characteristic of myeloma, but Bence Jones protein is the urine finding. Tell: Bence Jones is urine.
Excess immunoglobulin M is the product of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, causing hyperviscosity. Tell: Bence Jones is a urine monoclonal protein.
Light chains (kappa and lambda) are measured in the blood and their ratio is checked; that is a separate test. Tell: Bence Jones is the monoclonal protein found in the urine.

Correct. A positive urine monoclonal protein is called Bence Jones protein, found with the 24-hour urine protein electrophoresis. A monoclonal protein on serum protein electrophoresis is characteristic of myeloma.

set2.q: About what share of non-Hodgkin lymphomas are B-cell lymphomas?

Fifteen percent is the T-cell or natural killer-cell share, not the B-cell share. Tell: B-cell lymphomas are the large majority.
The split is not even; B-cell types make up about 85%. Tell: the T-cell and natural killer-cell types are the minority at 15%.

Correct. About 85% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas are B-cell and 15% are T-cell or natural killer-cell. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is a diverse group of lymphoid malignancies that present frequently with lymphadenopathy.

set2.q: Which is the more aggressive form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma?
opts: Marginal zone lymphoma is not a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma; the named aggressive form of skin T-cell lymphoma is Sezary syndrome, with erythroderma. Tell: a skin T-cell lymphoma's aggressive form is Sezary syndrome.
Anaplastic large cell lymphoma is an aggressive T-cell lymphoma, but it is not the named aggressive cutaneous form. Tell: red itchy erythroderma means Sezary syndrome.
Correct. Sezary syndrome is the more aggressive form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with a widespread, red, itchy rash (erythroderma) that may cause severe pruritus and a diminished quality of life.

Mycosis fungoides is the cutaneous T-cell lymphoma itself, skin lesions resembling fungal infection that can progress to ulcerating nodules. Tell: the more aggressive form with erythroderma is Sezary syndrome.

opts: Correct. Low-grade B-cell lymphomas are treated with rituximab, an anti-cluster of differentiation 20 monoclonal antibody, if treatment is required, with chemotherapy added if the disease is extensive.

Ibrutinib is a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor, a targeted therapy for chronic lymphocytic leukemia; low-grade B-cell lymphoma is treated with rituximab. Tell: for a low-grade B-cell lymphoma needing treatment, the named agent is rituximab.

Bleomycin is part of the Hodgkin lymphoma regimen (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine), and novel agents are replacing it because of pulmonary toxicities. Tell: bleomycin is Hodgkin; rituximab is low-grade B-cell lymphoma.
Allopurinol is a hypouricemic agent to prevent tumor lysis syndrome, not a lymphoma therapy. Tell: it protects the kidneys; rituximab treats the lymphoma.

set2.q: In the lymphoma work-up, what does an elevated lactate dehydrogenase reflect?
opts: A monoclonal protein on serum protein electrophoresis is characteristic of multiple myeloma. Tell: lactate dehydrogenase tracks proliferation, not a paraprotein.

Correct. The work-up includes LDH (lactate dehydrogenase), which reflects rapid proliferation, alongside a complete blood count for cytopenias from marrow involvement and chemistries to rule out tumor lysis syndrome.
Bone marrow involvement shows as cytopenias on the complete blood count. Tell: cytopenias reflect the marrow; lactate dehydrogenase reflects rapid proliferation.
Hyperviscosity comes from excess immunoglobulin M in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, not from lactate dehydrogenase. Tell: the enzyme marks fast cell turnover.

set2.q: In the Lugano staging of lymphoma, involved lymph node regions both above and below the diaphragm are which stage?

Stage 2 is two or more node regions on the same side of the diaphragm. Tell: crossing the diaphragm moves it to stage 3.

Correct. In the Lugano classification (a modified Ann Arbor system), stage 3 is two or more lymph node regions above and below the diaphragm. Stage 2 keeps them on the same side; stage 4 is widespread disease in multiple organs.
Stage 4 is widespread disease with multiple organs involved, with or without nodes. Tell: nodes on both sides without organ spread stop at stage 3.

set2.q: An M-protein of 1.5 g/dL, clonal marrow plasma cells of 4% and no anemia, bone lesions or renal failure fit which disorder?
opts: Active multiple myeloma with end-organ damage
Myeloma needs 10% or more marrow plasma cells or a plasmacytoma plus a CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) feature. Tell: 4% and no end-organ damage rule it out.
ruled out by a stated finding

Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma) results in excess immunoglobulin M, a large antibody that causes hyperviscosity. Tell: no immunoglobulin M or hyperviscosity is given; the numbers fit the low-level plasma cell disorder.

Correct. An M-protein below 3 g/dL (1.5 g/dL), clonal marrow plasma cells below 10% (4%) and no myeloma-defining characteristics meet every part of MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance), which progresses at about 1% per year.

opts: Correct. In the CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) features, hypercalcemia causes constipation, increased thirst, urinary frequency and nausea. Renal insufficiency causes swelling and anemia causes fatigue and shortness of breath.
Swelling is the symptom linked to renal insufficiency, the R of CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions). Tell: swelling is renal; constipation and thirst are calcium.
Fatigue and shortness of breath reflect anemia, the A of CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions). Tell: those are anemia symptoms, not calcium symptoms.
Pain in the back, chest or pelvis reflects bone lesions, the B of CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions). Tell: bone pain is the B; constipation and thirst are the C.

set2.q: Which organ enlargement is most often found on exam in chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: A nasal-region mass points to extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, not chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: this leukemia enlarges the spleen in about 40%.
Correct. On exam, splenomegaly is found in about 40% of patients, while hepatomegaly is less common. Painless, firm, mobile lymphadenopathy (50-90% of cases) is the other common finding on exam.
Hepatomegaly can occur but is less common than splenomegaly (about 40%). Tell: the spleen is the organ enlarged most often here.

Bulky disease, not non-bulky early disease, gives inferior results. Tell: small, early disease does well.
Cervical nodes are the usual presentation and carry no stated adverse meaning. Tell: the adverse groups are older age, bulk and certain subtypes.

Correct. Inferior results are seen with older patients, those with bulky disease and those with certain subtypes (lymphocyte depleted or mixed cellularity). Hodgkin lymphoma is otherwise generally curable.

set2.q: What proportion of Hodgkin lymphoma patients are alive at 5 years?
opts: About 50% is far below the outlook of Hodgkin lymphoma, which is generally curable. Tell: Hodgkin is generally curable, over 90% at 5 years.
About 60% is the 5-year relative survival of multiple myeloma. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma does better, over 90%.
About 78% is the relative 5-year survival of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma survival exceeds 90%.
Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma is generally curable, with more than 90% of patients alive at 5 years. Relapse after first-line treatment may require allogeneic stem cell transplant.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set2.q: How is smoldering myeloma usually managed?
opts: Autologous transplant improves survival in transplant-eligible active myeloma. Tell: smoldering disease is usually monitored, not transplanted.
Allopurinol and fluids are given in advance in aggressive lymphoma, where tumor lysis syndrome should be anticipated. Tell: smoldering myeloma usually needs no treatment at all.
Correct. Smoldering myeloma typically does not require treatment, though early intervention may be considered for some subgroups. It progresses at about 10% per year, faster in some high-risk groups.
A 3- or 4-drug regimen is for newly diagnosed, symptomatic multiple myeloma. Tell: smoldering has no myeloma-defining events and is usually not treated.

set2.q: Which infection can cause an atypical lymphocytosis that mimics chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: Correct. Atypical lymphocytosis can be seen with some infections, including pertussis, so an infection-related rise belongs in the differential of a high lymphocyte count before chronic lymphocytic leukemia is called.
Helicobacter pylori gastritis is tied to gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma in two thirds of cases, not to a reactive lymphocytosis. Tell: H. pylori means gastric lymphoma.

Hepatitis C is associated with splenic marginal zone lymphoma and is listed among the chronic infections that are non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk factors, not the named cause of atypical lymphocytosis. Tell: the mimic named is pertussis.
Lyme disease is listed among the chronic infections that raise non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk. Tell: a reactive lymphocytosis mimic here is pertussis.

set2.topic: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia: who and why
set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set2.q: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a proliferation of which cell type?
opts: Correct. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a proliferative leukemia of mature B-cell lymphocytes found in the blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen. Mutagenesis occurs in mature B cells, which is why the disease presents as a clonal population.
Immature lymphoblasts are not the cell of this disease: chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a proliferative leukemia of mature B-cell lymphocytes. Tell: match the word mature, and the B-cell lineage.

Mature T-cell leukemias exist but are rare and carry another name, T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia itself is a B-cell disease. Tell: the common chronic lymphocytic leukemia is B-cell; the T-cell form is rare and named separately.

Clonal plasma cells, terminally differentiated B cells, define the plasma cell disorders such as multiple myeloma, not chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: myeloma arises from plasma cells; this leukemia is a proliferation of mature B lymphocytes.

set2.q: Which presentation fits primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma?
opts: Blurred vision and headache come from immunoglobulin M hyperviscosity in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Tell: thick blood blurs vision; a mediastinal mass causes cough.

Correct. Primary mediastinal B-cell lymphomas present with a large mediastinal mass, cough and an abnormal chest X-ray. Central nervous system lymphoma, by contrast, presents with headaches, lethargy and neurologic deficits.
Headaches, lethargy and neurologic deficits that mirror primary brain tumors describe central nervous system lymphoma. Tell: mediastinal disease shows in the chest.
Widespread red itchy erythroderma is Sezary syndrome, a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Tell: a mediastinal B-cell lymphoma is a chest mass.

Acute lymphocytic leukemia 2. Acute myelogenous leukemia 3. Lymphoma 4. Hodgkin 5. Non-Hodgkin
set2.q: What is the usual management of follicular lymphoma that causes no symptoms?
opts: Multi-agent chemotherapy is the approach to aggressive B-cell lymphomas. Tell: an asymptomatic indolent lymphoma is watched; intensive therapy is kept for high-risk disease.
Rapid transfer of care is required for Burkitt lymphoma, whose doubling time is extremely fast. Tell: emergency transfer is for Burkitt, not an indolent lymphoma.
Allogeneic stem cell transplant may be required for Hodgkin lymphoma that relapses after first-line treatment. Tell: asymptomatic follicular lymphoma is observed.

Correct. Follicular lymphoma frequently needs no treatment (watch and wait), though it may be treated with intermittent low-intensity therapy if symptomatic; high-risk disease may need more aggressive therapy. It is incurable, but often needs no treatment or only intermittent treatment.

set2.q: How is the lymphadenopathy of chronic lymphocytic leukemia described?
opts: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia nodes are painless, not tender or fluctuant. Tell: the classic node here is painless, firm and mobile.
Node pain that worsens with alcohol is a feature of Hodgkin lymphoma, not chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: alcohol-related node pain points to Hodgkin lymphoma.

Waxing and waning painless lymphadenopathy is the typical indolent presentation of follicular lymphoma. Tell: waxing and waning means follicular; firm, mobile, painless nodes with lymphocytosis mean chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
Correct. Painless lymphadenopathy occurs in 50-90% of cases and may be localized or generalized; the nodes are firm and mobile. Splenomegaly is found in about 40% and hepatomegaly less often.

set2.q: Which statement describes the prognosis of indolent lymphomas?
opts: Correct. Indolent lymphomas are incurable but survival is often 10-15 or more years with intermittent treatment, with a risk of progression to an aggressive, difficult-to-treat lymphoma. Aggressive lymphomas, by contrast, are often treatable.
Curable in about half with chemotherapy
Cure with chemotherapy describes aggressive lymphomas, not indolent ones, which stay incurable even with treatment. Tell: aggressive lymphomas can be cured; indolent ones are incurable but slow.
More than 90% alive at 5 years describes Hodgkin lymphoma, which is generally curable. Tell: that is Hodgkin, not an indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Survival under 2 years is not the outlook for indolent lymphomas; patients often survive 10-15 or more years. Tell: indolent means incurable but slow.

set2.q: In the Rai classification, lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, with normal hemoglobin and platelets, is which stage?
opts: Stage I is lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy only. Tell: an enlarged spleen counts as organomegaly and moves the stage to II.
Correct. Rai stage II is lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy and organomegaly, defined as hepatomegaly and/or splenomegaly. With no anemia and no thrombocytopenia, the stage does not rise to III or IV.
Stage III requires anemia. Tell: the hemoglobin is normal, so organomegaly alone stops at stage II.
Stage IV requires thrombocytopenia. Tell: the platelets are normal, so the stage cannot reach IV.

set2.q: For a transplant candidate with multiple myeloma, which step has been shown to improve overall survival?
opts: Correct. If the patient is a transplant candidate, autologous transplant has been shown to improve overall survival, as has maintenance therapy after transplant. Most patients still relapse and need continuous therapy.

Allogeneic stem cell transplant is not the survival-improving step named for myeloma; it is named for Hodgkin lymphoma that relapses after first-line treatment. Tell: myeloma uses the patient's own cells, autologous.
Most myeloma patients relapse and need continuous therapy, and maintenance after transplant improves survival. Tell: therapy continues; it is not stopped at remission.
Radiation of each lesion is not described as a survival-improving step. Tell: the survival benefit comes from autologous transplant and maintenance.

set2.q: Which antibody type is most commonly overproduced in multiple myeloma?
opts: Immunoglobulin M is the monoclonal protein that Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia often produces, a different disorder in the myeloma differential. Tell: M is Waldenstrom; G is myeloma.
Immunoglobulin E is not named as a myeloma protein; the most common is immunoglobulin G. Tell: G is the usual myeloma antibody.
Immunoglobulin A is not the antibody named; myeloma most commonly overproduces immunoglobulin G. Tell: most commonly G.
Correct. Clonal evolution of myeloma produces a single, overproduced antibody type, most commonly immunoglobulin G. Normal plasma cells are responsible for producing antibodies.

set2.q: Which virus is a suspected risk factor found in 40-50% of Hodgkin lymphoma cases?
opts: Correct. Epstein-Barr virus is suspected as a risk factor and is identified in 40-50% of Hodgkin lymphoma cases. Others include human immunodeficiency virus, human herpesvirus 6 and tuberculosis.
Hepatitis C is associated with splenic marginal zone lymphoma. Tell: the Hodgkin virus found in about half of cases is Epstein-Barr.
Human T-lymphotropic virus 1 is associated with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Tell: Hodgkin is a B-cell lymphoma, and Epstein-Barr virus is its suspected virus.
Human herpesvirus 8 is on the non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk list; the herpesvirus named for Hodgkin is type 6, and the main suspect is Epstein-Barr virus. Tell: 40-50% of cases carry Epstein-Barr virus.
